text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game: each token kept privately earns me 1 point but costs others 0.75 each, while tokens in the group account give me only 0.75 per token with no penalty to others—so I'm setting up the formula combining my own private holdings, others' private holdings, and the group total.

Computing the group-optimal outcome, I find that total welfare is maximized when everyone contributes everything to the group account (P=0), yielding 60 points total versus the dominant individual strategy of keeping tokens private, since the marginal private return still outweighs the group return per person.

This is the classic public goods dilemma where defection dominates but full cooperation is socially optimal. Given it's a repeated 10-round game, I think signaling cooperation early makes sense, so I'll contribute my full 20 tokens in round one to see how others respond.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure: each token kept privately earns me 1 point but costs each of the other three members 0.75, while each token put into the group account earns me only 0.75 with no harm to others—so I'm comparing the private incentive against the collective benefit of cooperation.

Since private tokens yield 1 for self versus 0.75 for group, keeping tokens private is the dominant individual strategy, even though it's worse for total group welfare (private nets -1.25 overall versus +0.75 for group contributions). This creates the classic social dilemma where individual rationality undermines collective outcomes.

Given this is a repeated 10-round game with 4 members, I'm leaning toward opening with full cooperation (contributing all 20 tokens) to signal good faith and test how others respond, since I'll be able to gauge the group's total contribution over time even without seeing individual choices.

Comparing totals, if everyone keeps all 20 tokens, each person nets 20 - 45 = -25 due to the externalities from others' keeping, whereas if everyone contributes all 20, each nets a clean 15. So full cooperation is clearly the socially better outcome, even though keeping dominates individually when ignoring externalities.

Since this is a repeated 10-round public goods game, cooperation and reciprocity make sense strategically. I'll start by contributing all 20 tokens in round 1 and see how others respond.
